summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

primary_citations.citation_text: Maryland - Md. Code, Family Law Article §§ 5-701 et seq. (Child Abuse and Neglect; definitions at § 5-701, mandatory reporting at §§ 5-704 and 5-705, investigation at § 5-706, appeal of findings at § 5-706.1)
Maryland - Courts & Judicial Proc. § 3-801 et seq. (CINA—Child in Need of Assistance proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services for the City of Baltimore
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of most of a father's § 1983 claims against the Baltimore City department but held that his allegation that the State transferred custody of his son on an emergency basis and then denied him any hearing stated a procedural due process claim that could not be dismissed.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the constitutional floor for protective custody taken before judicial authorization.
key_cases.quote: Due process does not mandate a prior hearing in cases where emergency action may be needed to protect a child.

key_cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for Maryland caseworkers on qualified immunity, holding that the record showed at most negligent miscommunication causing an out-of-state removal, and that the mother's due process rights were not violated where a post-deprivation hearing occurred and the children were returned within 24 hours.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms the statutory basis in FL § 5-709(c) for emergency protective custody and the process that must follow.
key_cases.quote: Because a § 1983 claim cannot be sustained, it follows that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for Maryland officials, holding that investigative home visits by social workers are not measured by criminal-search standards and that the entry of the caseworker and accompanying deputies into a consenting foster mother's home was not unreasonable.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the search-and-seizure framework governing protective action taken at the home.
key_cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed rejection of facial and as-applied challenges to Virginia's 72-hour emergency-removal statute, holding that a 65-hour weekend delay in judicial review of a protective removal did not violate due process, while reversing dismissal of the parents' § 1983 claim against the county and its social services department arising from the removal itself.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes how long protective custody may last before judicial review without offending due process in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that section 63.1-248.9, as it was applied in this case so as to permit such a delay, does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Court of Special Appeals, the Court held that a mother could maintain an interlocutory appeal from the order awarding temporary custody of her CINA child to the father under departmental supervision, and that subsequent review-hearing orders that changed nothing did not render the appeal moot.
key_cases.relevance: It traces the Maryland sequence from emergency shelter care through CINA adjudication to custody orders, and secures review of the order that follows emergency action.
key_cases.quote: We shall hold that Petitioner had a right to an interlocutory appeal and that the appeal has not been rendered moot by orders issued at subsequent review hearings.

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-705(a)(1)
Health practitioners — Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-704(a)
Police officers — Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-704(a)
Educators or human service workers, including teachers, counselors, social workers, caseworkers, and probation or parole officers — Md. Code, Fam. Law §§ 5-704(a), 5-701(g)
Narrow exceptions to the any-person duty: attorney-client privilege, the constitutional right to counsel, and certain clergy confidences — Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-705(a)(2)-(3)
reporting_details: Maryland is a universal-reporter state: any person who has reason to believe a child has been abused or neglected must notify the local department of social services or the appropriate law enforcement agency, and a health practitioner, police officer, educator, or human service worker must also file a written report with the local department not later than 48 hours after the contact, with a copy to the local State's Attorney (Md. Code, Fam. Law §§ 5-704, 5-705).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours (suspected physical or sexual abuse); 5 days (suspected neglect or mental injury)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Report received by the local department or the appropriate law enforcement agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-706

timeline_requirements.deadline: 10 days to the extent possible; if not completed within 30 days, within 60 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the first notice of the suspected abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Md. Code, Fam. Law § 5-706
